note: Source-check dates preserve the checks recorded when these entries were maintained; they are not new replication checks. Source format and claim status are separate. Reported means the cited source reports the result or event, not that independent groups have confirmed it. Preliminary, disputed, and retracted flag the cautions recorded in each summary. Consult the source for methods, publication history, and subsequent updates.

items.title: 42 lost pages of the sixth-century Codex H recovered by multispectral imaging
items.authors: Garrick Allen (University of Glasgow) with the Early Manuscripts Electronic Library (EMEL)
items.venue: University of Glasgow / Codex H digital edition
items.summary: Codex H (Gregory-Aland 015) is a sixth-century Greek copy of Paul's letters that monks at the Great Lavra on Mount Athos took apart in the thirteenth century and reused as binding material, scattering its 41 surviving leaves across libraries in Italy, Greece, Russia, Ukraine and France. When the text was re-inked centuries ago, the new ink chemically 'offset' a mirror image onto facing pages; multispectral imaging (photographing under many wavelengths of light) made those ghost texts readable, effectively recovering 42 pages that no longer physically exist, and radiocarbon dating confirmed the sixth-century parchment. The recovered material includes the earliest known chapter lists for Paul's letters, part of the Euthalian apparatus, an ancient navigation system of prologues and headings. A free digital edition is online and a print edition is forthcoming, so peer scrutiny of the readings is still in progress.
items.headline: Multispectral imaging recovers lost pages of a sixth-century manuscript

items.title: Arolsen Archives and Ancestry index eight million names from Nazi concentration-camp lists
items.authors: Arolsen Archives - International Center on Nazi Persecution, with Ancestry
items.summary: The Arolsen Archives in Bad Arolsen, Germany, hold about 30 million original documents on Nazi persecution (a UNESCO Memory of the World collection), and their online archive now offers more than 40 million document images. For Holocaust Remembrance Day 2026 they announced that, with Ancestry, every name on the surviving concentration-camp transport and prisoner lists (over eight million entries, plus two million from correspondence files) has been fully indexed and is searchable free of charge; the data will be folded into the Arolsen online archive by 2027. Because the same person often appears on several lists, eight million names does not mean eight million people, but for many victims a single line on one list is the last trace that they existed.
items.headline: An archive project indexes millions of names from Nazi camp records

items.title: National Economy Pushed Forward with Innovation-led and High-quality Development and Expected Targets Achieved Successfully in 2025 (population section)
items.authors: National Bureau of Statistics of China
items.venue: NBS press release, State Council Information Office briefing
items.summary: China's official statistics agency reported that the population stood at 1,404.89 million at the end of 2025, down 3.39 million in a year, the fourth straight annual decline and the steepest yet. Births fell to 7.92 million (a birth rate of 5.63 per thousand, the lowest in the modern era) against 11.31 million deaths, giving a natural growth rate of minus 2.41 per thousand; 23.0 percent of the population is now aged 60 or over and 15.9 percent 65 or over, while 67.89 percent lives in cities. The figures frame the 'East Asia today' story of rapid ageing shared with Japan and South Korea. Demographers note that NBS annual estimates are sample-based between censuses and have been revised after past censuses, and some independent analysts believe births are overstated.
items.headline: China's official statistics report another year of population decline

items.title: An unfinished Pompeian construction site reveals ancient Roman building technology
items.authors: Vaserman, Weaver, Hayhow et al. (Pompeii Archaeological Park and MIT team)
items.summary: The new excavations in Pompeii's Regio IX (2023 onward) exposed a building site frozen mid-work by the AD 79 eruption, with tools, stacked tiles, tuff blocks and piles of lime and pozzolana (volcanic ash). Sampling in 2024-2025 and chemical analysis showed the Romans mixed quicklime with dry pozzolana before adding water: 'hot mixing', an exothermic process that leaves reactive lime lumps able to seal later cracks. This is field confirmation of the self-healing mechanism proposed from lab work on Roman mortars (Seymour et al., Science Advances, 2023). The same excavation campaign also uncovered a bakery-prison and richly frescoed rooms reported through the park's E-Journal.
items.headline: An unfinished Pompeii building reveals Roman construction methods

explainer.finding: An unfinished Pompeii building site preserves evidence of how Roman builders prepared concrete materials, supporting a hot-mixing interpretation.
explainer.method: Researchers combined archaeological context with analysis of construction materials and their chemical and microscopic characteristics.
explainer.meaning: A site interrupted during work can reveal steps that are harder to reconstruct from a finished wall. It connects material chemistry with a historical building process.
explainer.limits: One site does not describe every Roman workshop. Evidence about preparation also differs from measuring the long-term performance of every resulting structure.

items.title: Lost Anglo-Saxon village uncovered near Friston, Suffolk, on the East Anglia TWO route
items.authors: MOLA-Wessex Archaeology for ScottishPower Renewables
items.summary: Ninety archaeologists excavating more than 24 hectares ahead of an offshore-wind cable route found an early medieval settlement of seven or eight timber longhouses, some 19 metres long, about 12 miles from the Sutton Hoo royal burials. Nothing in the written record placed a village here, and a modern public footpath runs exactly along the line of the buildings, suggesting the path has been walked since Anglo-Saxon times. Because ordinary rural settlements of this period are far rarer in the record than elite graves, the site should help balance the picture of how most people in the East Anglian kingdom actually lived; dating, finds analysis and publication are still under way.
items.headline: Excavation uncovers an Anglo-Saxon village in Suffolk

items.title: Ancient DNA from Shimao city records kinship practices in Neolithic China
items.authors: Zehui Chen, Jacob D. Gardner, Zhouyong Sun, E. Andrew Bennett, Qian Han et al.
items.summary: Researchers sequenced 144 ancient genomes from Shimao, a 4,000-year-old walled stone city on the Loess Plateau of northern Shaanxi (c. 2300-1800 BCE), and from nearby settlements. The Shimao population descended mainly from earlier Yangshao farming groups with continuing input from Inner Mongolia, and the burials show a predominantly patrilineal (father-to-son) descent structure. Genetic and isotopic evidence also suggests that the young women whose skulls fill Shimao's sacrificial pits were outsiders, hinting at sex-specific ritual killing. The study is the first large-scale genetic portrait of an early Chinese proto-state and shows kinship, not just wealth, structured its elite.
items.headline: Ancient DNA investigates kinship in the Neolithic city of Shimao

items.title: Cundill History Prize 2025: Lyndal Roper, Summer of Fire and Blood: The German Peasants' War
items.authors: Lyndal Roper (Regius Professor of History, University of Oxford)
items.summary: The US$75,000 Cundill Prize, the world's richest award for a history book, went to Roper's account of the 1524-25 German Peasants' War, the largest popular uprising in Europe before the French Revolution, in which perhaps 100,000 rebels were killed. Roper reads the revolt as a coherent mass movement rooted in Reformation ideas of Christian freedom and the common good, rather than the chaotic outburst that Luther condemned and later historians often echoed. Runners-up Marlene L. Daut and Sophia Rosenfeld each received US$10,000.
items.headline: The Cundill Prize recognizes a history of the German Peasants' War

items.title: Paratyphoid fever and relapsing fever in 1812 Napoleon's devastated army
items.authors: Rémi Barbieri, Julien Fumey, Helja Kabral, Christiana Lyn Scheib, Michel Signoli, Caroline Costedoat, Nicolás Rascovan
items.summary: DNA from the teeth of 13 soldiers in a Vilnius mass grave from the December 1812 retreat from Moscow (a site holding more than 3,000 bodies with no battle wounds) yielded Salmonella enterica Paratyphi C, which causes paratyphoid fever, in four men and the louse-borne bacterium Borrelia recurrentis, which causes relapsing fever, in two. Earlier PCR work had blamed typhus and trench fever; the new shotgun-sequencing approach did not find those, so the study widens rather than settles the list of diseases that helped destroy the Grande Armée. Thirteen individuals is a small sample, and absence of a pathogen in degraded DNA is not proof it was absent from the army.
items.headline: Pathogen evidence revisits disease in Napoleon's retreating army

items.title: One Trillion Web Pages Archived: the Wayback Machine passes a civilization-scale milestone
items.authors: Internet Archive (Brewster Kahle, founder; blog post by Caralee Adams)
items.summary: In October 2025 the Internet Archive's Wayback Machine, which has captured web pages since 1996, passed one trillion archived pages, marked by a celebration in San Francisco on 22 October. The Archive also reported preserving more than 400 million US government web pages through the End of Term Web Archive and repairing over 28 million broken citation links on Wikipedia. For historians the web archive is becoming the primary source base for the late twentieth and twenty-first centuries, and the milestone highlights both the scale of born-digital evidence and its fragility: the Archive faces ongoing lawsuits and funding pressures, so the record is not guaranteed to survive.
items.headline: The Wayback Machine reaches a trillion archived web pages

items.title: 2025 John K. Fairbank Prize in East Asian History awarded to Matthew H. Sommer for The Fox Spirit, the Stone Maiden, and Other Transgender Histories from Late Imperial China
items.authors: American Historical Association
items.summary: The American Historical Association's Fairbank Prize, the leading US book award for East Asian history since 1800, went in 2025 to Stanford historian Matthew H. Sommer for a study (Columbia University Press, 2024) that uses Qing legal case records to recover the lives of people who crossed gender boundaries in late imperial China, from men living as women to 'stone maidens' (women who could not consummate marriage). The book argues that Qing law and society had categories for such people that do not map neatly onto modern Western ones. The 2024 prize went to Tristan G. Brown (MIT) for Laws of the Land: Fengshui and the State in Qing Dynasty China (Princeton, 2023), which showed how geomantic claims shaped property and mining disputes in Qing courts; together the two awards signal the field's turn toward legal archives as social history.
items.headline: The Fairbank Prize recognizes a study of transgender histories in late imperial China

items.title: Qin structural timbers and the First Emperor's Mausoleum (Xi'an, China)
items.authors: Ying Yang, Dorian Q. Fuller, Andrew Bevan, Xiuzhen Li, Wenbin Shao, Yin Xia
items.summary: Anthracology (identifying wood species from charcoal) of 657 charred timbers from four pits at the mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang, home of the Terracotta Army, shows that 94 percent were conifers, mostly fir, spruce and hemlock that grow only high in the Qinling Mountains far from the tomb. Earlier pits used lower-elevation cypress, later ones increasingly high-altitude species, suggesting nearby forests were exhausted as construction went on. The pattern documents the logistical reach and environmental cost of the Qin state's building program (c. 246-208 BCE). It complements ongoing excavation of Pit 2, where a rare officer figure was recovered in late 2024; the emperor's own burial mound remains deliberately unexcavated.
items.headline: Structural timber provides evidence about the First Emperor's mausoleum

items.title: Evidence for deliberate burial of the dead by Homo naledi
items.authors: Lee R. Berger, Tebogo Makhubela, Keneiloe Molopyane et al.
items.summary: Berger's team argues that Homo naledi, a small-brained hominin living in South Africa's Rising Star cave system some 241,000 to 335,000 years ago, deliberately buried its dead, which would push intentional burial back by 100,000 years or more and detach it from large brains. First posted as a reviewed preprint in 2023, the paper drew sharp criticism; Martinón-Torres and colleagues (Journal of Human Evolution, 2024) concluded there was no scientific evidence for burial or rock art. A revised version of record appeared in September 2025, but eLife's assessment records the reviewers split between 'convincing' and 'incomplete', so the claim remains contested.
items.headline: Researchers debate evidence for deliberate burial by Homo naledi

items.title: Guiding Principles for Artificial Intelligence in History Education
items.authors: American Historical Association, Ad Hoc Committee on Artificial Intelligence in History Education
items.venue: American Historical Association (approved by Council 29 July 2025)
items.summary: The largest professional body of historians in the United States issued its first formal position on generative AI, drawing on a 2024 survey of members. The principles hold that historical thinking is a human skill AI cannot replace, that language models generate plausible patterns rather than truths and routinely invent sources and quotations, that bans are impractical so critical AI literacy should be taught, that syllabi need explicit and transparent AI policies, and that 'there are no shortcuts to expertise'. Critics argued the document stops short of tackling AI in research and archives, but it is the clearest statement so far of how the discipline intends to police the new tools.
items.headline: Historians propose principles for using AI in history education

items.title: Contextualizing ancient texts with generative neural networks (Aeneas)
items.authors: Yannis Assael, Thea Sommerschield, et al. (Google DeepMind with the Universities of Nottingham, Warwick, Oxford and AUEB)
items.summary: Aeneas is a neural network trained on more than 176,000 Latin inscriptions that restores missing letters, estimates where an inscription was made (72% accuracy across 62 Roman provinces) and when (on average within 13 years of scholars' date ranges), and, most usefully, retrieves 'parallels', other inscriptions with similar wording or formulae, in seconds. It succeeds Ithaca, the same team's 2022 Nature model for Greek inscriptions. Epigraphy (the study of inscriptions) is one of the main sources for Roman social history, so a tool that surfaces comparanda at scale changes how historians work; in a test of 23 historians the model was judged helpful for 90% of inscriptions, though the authors stress it is a research aid, not a replacement for expert judgement.
items.headline: Aeneas uses neural networks to help place ancient texts in context

items.title: First title and author read from a still-rolled Herculaneum scroll: Philodemus, On Vices (PHerc. 172)
items.authors: Vesuvius Challenge team; Marcel Roth and Micha Nowak; Sean Johnson
items.summary: Using X-ray CT scans and machine-learning ink detection, the Vesuvius Challenge read the title of a carbonized papyrus scroll from Herculaneum without unrolling it: PHerc. 172, held at Oxford's Bodleian Libraries, is On Vices by the Epicurean philosopher Philodemus (1st century BC). It follows the 2023 first-word ('porphyras', purple) and grand-prize readings and is the first time a rolled Herculaneum scroll has been identified non-invasively. The papyrologists confirmed author and title, but the book number is less certain; the results are announcements by the competition rather than a peer-reviewed publication.
items.headline: Readers identify an author and title in a still-rolled Herculaneum scroll

items.title: The genetic origin of the Indo-Europeans
items.authors: Iosif Lazaridis, Nick Patterson, David W. Anthony et al.
items.summary: Genome data from 435 ancient individuals identified a 'Caucasus-Lower Volga' (CLV) population, a genetic gradient (cline) blending Caucasus hunter-gatherer ancestry with eastern European hunter-gatherer ancestry between roughly 4400 and 4000 BC. CLV people contributed about four-fifths of the ancestry of the Yamnaya, the steppe pastoralists whose expansion after 3300 BC is linked with the spread of most Indo-European languages, and also appear to have contributed to Bronze Age Anatolians. This offers a single genetic source that could reconcile the Anatolian branch with the rest of the family, though equating genes with languages remains an inference, not proof.
items.headline: Ancient DNA investigates the ancestry associated with Indo-European expansion

items.title: Pan-European atmospheric lead pollution, enhanced blood lead levels, and cognitive decline from Roman-era mining and smelting
items.authors: Joseph R. McConnell, Nathan J. Chellman, Andreas Plach et al.
items.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
items.summary: Lead trapped in Arctic ice cores records the fallout from Roman silver and lead mining and smelting; atmospheric modelling converted it into estimated air concentrations across Europe during the Pax Romana (roughly 27 BC to AD 180). Applying modern dose-response relationships, the authors estimate childhood blood lead was raised by about 2.4 micrograms per decilitre, enough for an average IQ reduction of roughly 2.5 to 3 points across the empire. It is the first quantitative estimate of empire-wide health effects from ancient industrial pollution, though translating modern epidemiology to ancient populations involves assumptions.
items.headline: A model estimates exposure to lead pollution from Roman mining

items.title: Tsinghua University Warring States Bamboo Manuscripts, Volume 14 (Qinghua daxue cang Zhanguo zhujian, shisi)
items.authors: Tsinghua University Research and Conservation Center for Excavated Texts (eds.)
items.venue: Zhongxi Book Company (Shanghai); launch at Tsinghua University
items.summary: The Tsinghua bamboo slips are about 2,500 Warring States-period (c. 300 BCE) manuscripts acquired by Tsinghua University in 2008, the largest such collection known. Volume 14 publishes three previously unknown texts: 'Cheng Hou' and 'Zhao Hou', which record the political thought of the early Western Zhou kings Cheng and Zhao, and 'Liang Zhong', a long dialogue involving Yu and Qi, the legendary founders of the Xia dynasty, which Chinese scholars read as the earliest text calling Qi 'king of all under heaven'. Because the slips were bought on the antiquities market rather than excavated, some Western scholars treat their provenance cautiously, though physical testing and content have led most specialists to accept them as genuine.
items.headline: A new volume publishes Warring States bamboo manuscripts

items.title: Neanderthal ancestry through time: Insights from genomes of ancient and present-day humans
items.authors: Leonardo N. M. Iasi, Manjusha Chintalapati, Laurits Skov et al.
items.summary: By tracking Neanderthal DNA segments in more than 300 ancient and modern human genomes, the study dates the main interbreeding between Neanderthals and modern humans to a single extended period of roughly 50,500 to 43,500 years ago, lasting about 7,000 years. Natural selection then quickly removed some Neanderthal variants and favoured others, shaping the pattern still visible in people outside Africa today. A companion Nature paper (Sümer et al., 2024) on 45,000-year-old genomes from Ranis, Germany, and Zlatý kůň, Czechia, independently narrows the admixture to around 45,000 to 49,000 years ago.
items.headline: Ancient genomes refine the history of Neanderthal ancestry

items.title: Clay cylinders from Umm el-Marra, Syria, claimed as the earliest alphabetic writing (c. 2400 BC)
items.authors: Glenn M. Schwartz (Johns Hopkins University)
items.venue: American Society of Overseas Research annual meeting (conference presentation)
items.summary: Four finger-length clay cylinders from an Early Bronze Age tomb at Tell Umm el-Marra, radiocarbon dated to about 2400 BC, carry short sign sequences that Schwartz interprets as alphabetic writing, which would predate the Egyptian and Sinai inscriptions usually treated as the alphabet's origin by some 500 years. Epigrapher Christopher Rollston has backed the reading, but others such as Philippa Steele caution that a handful of very short, undeciphered texts cannot establish how many signs the system had or that it is alphabetic at all. The cylinders were first published in 2021; the 2024 presentation renewed attention, but no consensus exists.
items.headline: Clay cylinders prompt a claim for unusually early alphabetic writing

items.title: Seals and signs: tracing the origins of writing in ancient South-west Asia
items.authors: Kathryn Kelley, Mattia Cartolano, Silvia Ferrara
items.summary: Proto-cuneiform (c. 3350-3000 BC) is the earliest writing from Uruk in southern Iraq, and where its several hundred signs came from has been unclear. The Bologna team matched motifs on pre-literate cylinder seals used across Uruk-period trade networks, such as fringed textiles, vessels in nets, temple facades and poles, to specific proto-cuneiform signs for the same goods and institutions. The result suggests seal imagery for tracking commodities was one direct source of the writing system, though sign-by-sign identifications are interpretive and open to debate.
items.headline: Seal designs offer clues to the origins of writing

items.title: Running out of empty space: environmental lidar and the crowded ancient landscape of Campeche, Mexico
items.authors: Luke Auld-Thomas, Marcello A. Canuto, Adriana Velázquez Morlet et al.
items.summary: Re-analysing airborne lidar (laser scanning that maps ground surfaces beneath forest canopy) originally collected for an environmental survey, the team found 6,764 previously undocumented structures across about 122 square kilometres of Campeche. Among them is Valeriana, a large Classic Maya city with plazas, temple pyramids, a ballcourt and an E-Group assemblage suggesting a founding date before AD 150. The result supports the view that dense urban settlement was typical of the central Maya Lowlands rather than an artefact of where archaeologists happened to look.
items.headline: Lidar reveals a densely occupied ancient landscape in Mexico

items.title: Genetic analysis of a Yayoi individual from the Doigahama site provides insights into the origins of immigrants to the Japanese Archipelago
items.authors: Jonghyun Kim, Fuzuki Mizuno, Takayuki Matsushita, Masami Matsushita, Saki Aoto et al., Jun Ohashi
items.summary: A whole nuclear genome from a Yayoi-period skeleton (c. 2,000 years old) at Doigahama in Yamaguchi Prefecture carried three ancestries: indigenous Jomon hunter-gatherer, East Asian farmer and Northeast Siberian, the same mixture seen in later Kofun-period and modern Japanese. Comparison with ancient populations shows the closest match to people of the Korean Peninsula, indicating that most immigrants who brought rice farming and metal to Japan during the Yayoi and Kofun periods (c. 1000 BCE-538 CE) came via Korea. The result refines the 'tripartite' model of Japanese origins proposed in 2021 and, together with a January 2026 Scientific Reports study of Kyushu Yayoi genomes, supports gradual admixture over centuries rather than a single migration wave.
items.headline: A Yayoi genome adds evidence about migration to Japan

items.title: The collapse of the Ming Dynasty actually began with the Wanli megadrought: Insights from a hydroclimate reconstruction based on tree-ring δ18O over the past 460 years
items.authors: Meng Ren, Yu Liu, Qiufang Cai, Qiang Li, Huiming Song, Changfeng Sun
items.summary: Oxygen isotopes in tree rings from the southwestern Loess Plateau were used to reconstruct summer drought severity year by year from 1556 to 2015. Alongside the well-known Chongzhen drought of the 1630s-40s that preceded the Ming collapse in 1644, the record reveals a 'Wanli megadrought' of 1585-1590, as long and severe but barely mentioned in earlier historical work. The authors argue that this earlier drought, during the Little Ice Age and linked to El Nino-driven weakening of the Asian summer monsoon, began the fiscal and social unravelling of the Ming decades before the final crisis. Historians generally accept climate as one stressor among many; the claim that the collapse 'began' in the 1580s rests on a single regional proxy and remains an interpretation.
items.headline: Tree rings link severe drought with pressures on the Ming dynasty

items.title: Notre-Dame lead sarcophagus 'horseman' proposed as the poet Joachim du Bellay
items.authors: Inrap (Institut national de recherches archéologiques préventives) with the Toulouse forensic institute; Christophe Besnier, Éric Crubézy
items.venue: Inrap press briefing on Notre-Dame archaeology, Paris
items.summary: Rebuilding after the 2019 fire let archaeologists dig beneath the cathedral's transept crossing in 2022, where they found two lead coffins. One held Canon Antoine de La Porte (d. 1710), named on a plaque; the other, an anonymous man in his thirties whose pelvis showed years of riding and whose bones bore tuberculosis and chronic meningitis. In September 2024 Inrap proposed he is the Renaissance poet Joachim du Bellay (1522-1560), a horseman known to have been buried at Notre-Dame and to have suffered those illnesses. Tooth isotopes pointing to a Paris or Lyon childhood rather than Anjou, and the absence of any comparative DNA, keep the identification provisional.
items.headline: A Notre-Dame burial prompts a proposed identification with a Renaissance poet

items.title: A Scottish provenance for the Altar Stone of Stonehenge
items.authors: Anthony J. I. Clarke, Christopher L. Kirkland, Richard E. Bevins et al.
items.summary: The six-tonne Altar Stone at the centre of Stonehenge was long assumed to come from Wales like the other 'bluestones'. Dating tiny grains of zircon, apatite and rutile in the sandstone (detrital minerals carried into the rock when it formed) produced an age fingerprint matching the Old Red Sandstone of the Orcadian Basin in north-east Scotland, at least 750 km away. This implies Neolithic Britons moved a massive stone over an unprecedented distance, probably by sea, pointing to long-range coordination around 2500 BC; the exact quarry remains unidentified.
items.headline: Stonehenge's Altar Stone is traced to Scotland

items.title: European business cycles and economic growth, 1300–2000
items.authors: Stephen Broadberry, Jason Lennard
items.summary: Drawing on the reconstructed historical national accounts for nine European economies that underpin the 'Little Divergence' debate (the pulling ahead of England and the Low Countries from Italy and Spain after the Black Death), the authors date business cycles across seven centuries. Before 1800 economies lurched between short expansions and frequent, deep contractions driven by harvests, plague and war; the modern pattern of long expansions punctuated by brief recessions, synchronised across borders, only emerged in the nineteenth century alongside sustained growth and integrated markets. Pre-1800 GDP series carry wide error bands, so precise turning points for the medieval and early modern centuries should be read as indicative.
items.headline: Historical estimates reconstruct centuries of European economic growth

items.title: Island-wide characterization of agricultural production challenges the demographic collapse hypothesis for Rapa Nui (Easter Island)
items.authors: Dylan S. Davis, Robert J. DiNapoli, Gina Pakarati et al.
items.summary: Satellite imagery and machine learning mapped the island's rock gardens (fields mulched with broken stone to retain moisture and nutrients) and found far less agricultural land than earlier estimates, implying the pre-contact population was only a few thousand rather than the 15,000 or more assumed by the 'ecocide' collapse story. Ancient genomes published the same year (Moreno-Mayar et al., Nature, 2024) likewise show a small but steadily growing population with no genetic bottleneck before European contact in 1722. Together they undercut the popular narrative of self-inflicted collapse, though some archaeologists still argue for larger earlier populations.
items.headline: Land-use evidence challenges a population-collapse story for Rapa Nui

items.title: Widespread horse-based mobility arose around 2200 BCE in Eurasia
items.authors: Pablo Librado, Gaetan Tressières, Lorelei Chauvey, Antoine Fages, Naveed Khan, et al., Ludovic Orlando
items.summary: From 475 ancient horse genomes the authors dated the domestication bottleneck of the modern horse lineage to about 2700 BCE and found that deliberate breeding, seen as close-kin mating and shorter generation times, took off around 2200 BCE, when this lineage spread rapidly across Eurasia and replaced almost all local horses. That is centuries later than the Yamnaya steppe migrations of about 3000 BCE, so the paper argues those migrations were not carried out on large domesticated horse herds, as long assumed. The finding sits in tension with a 2023 Science Advances study reporting skeletal signs of riding in Yamnaya individuals, so exactly when riding began remains debated.
items.headline: Ancient DNA dates the spread of widespread horse-based mobility

items.title: Rice's trajectory from wild to domesticated in East Asia
items.authors: Jianping Zhang, Leping Jiang, Lupeng Yu, Xiujia Huan, Liping Zhou et al.
items.summary: Using phytoliths (microscopic silica bodies that preserve the shape of plant cells) from the Shangshan and Hehuashan sites in the lower Yangtze, the team traced rice through four stages: wild rice growing at least 100,000 years ago, gathering by about 24,000 years ago, cultivation before domestication about 13,000 years ago, and domestication about 11,000 years ago. This is the longest continuous record of any cereal's path to domestication and puts East Asian rice on the same timeline as wheat and barley in the Fertile Crescent. Some archaeobotanists caution that phytolith proxies for domestication are indirect and that 'domestication' here is a threshold in a gradual process rather than a single event.
items.headline: Research traces the long path from wild rice to domestication

items.title: The Egyptian pyramid chain was built along the now abandoned Ahramat Nile Branch
items.authors: Eman Ghoneim, Timothy J. Ralph, Suzanne Onstine et al.
items.summary: Radar satellite imagery, geophysical survey and sediment cores revealed a buried former branch of the Nile, named the Ahramat ('pyramids') Branch, running for tens of kilometres along the desert edge past 31 pyramids from Lisht to Giza. Many pyramid causeways end at its former bank, suggesting the river was the highway for moving stone and workers during the Old and Middle Kingdoms. The branch later silted up and shifted east, which helps explain why the pyramids now stand in seemingly inhospitable desert; the timing of its migration is still being refined.
items.headline: A lost Nile branch helps explain the placement of Egyptian pyramids

items.title: Vesuvius Challenge Grand Prize: first passages read from an unopened Herculaneum scroll
items.authors: Youssef Nader, Luke Farritor, Julian Schilliger (winners); Brent Seales, Nat Friedman, Daniel Gross (organizers)
items.summary: The Herculaneum papyri were carbonized by the eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79 and crumble if unrolled. The Vesuvius Challenge, an open competition using synchrotron X-ray CT scans, awarded its $700,000 grand prize on 5 February 2024 to three students whose machine-learning ink detection recovered more than 2,000 characters (about 5% of one scroll) of a Greek Epicurean text on pleasure. Progress since: in May 2025 the title 'On Vices' by Philodemus was read from the still-rolled scroll PHerc. 172, twenty more scrolls were scanned in a single 2025 session, and in June 2026 the team announced the first scroll read from beginning to end, PHerc. 1667. The only library to survive from antiquity is starting to be read.
items.headline: A scanning challenge recovers text from an unopened Herculaneum scroll

items.title: Two thousand years of garden urbanism in the Upper Amazon
items.authors: Stéphen Rostain, Antoine Dorison, Geoffroy de Saulieu, Heiko Prümers, Jean-Luc Le Pennec, Fernando Mejía Mejía, Ana Maritza Freire, Jaime R. Pagán-Jiménez, Philippe Descola
items.summary: Airborne LiDAR (laser scanning that strips away forest canopy in the data) revealed more than 6,000 earthen platforms, plazas and straight roads in the Upano Valley of Amazonian Ecuador, occupied from about 500 BCE to 300–600 CE. The settlements were dense yet interwoven with fields and drainage, a pattern the authors call garden urbanism, and they are older than the well-known LiDAR-mapped sites in the Bolivian Amazon. Together with earlier lowland surveys, the study overturns the twentieth-century picture of pre-Columbian Amazonia as sparsely populated wilderness and shows how remote sensing is rewriting the map of ancient urbanism.
items.headline: Lidar reveals extensive ancient settlements in the Upper Amazon

items.title: Population genomics of post-glacial western Eurasia
items.authors: Morten E. Allentoft, Martin Sikora, Alba Refoyo-Martínez, Evan K. Irving-Pease, Anders Fischer, et al., Eske Willerslev
items.summary: The team sequenced 317 new ancient genomes, mostly Mesolithic and Neolithic hunter-gatherers and farmers, and combined them with published data to build a time series of more than 1,600 ancient Europeans and western Asians. They found a long-lived genetic 'great divide' running from the Black Sea to the Baltic that separated western hunter-gatherers from eastern ones for millennia, and they traced how incoming farmers and later steppe pastoralists replaced or mixed with local populations at different speeds in different regions. Ancient DNA at this scale turns prehistory from a story told through pots and tools into one that can be read in population movements, a shift that has reopened old debates about migration versus cultural diffusion.
items.headline: Ancient genomes map population changes after the last ice age

items.title: Wolfson History Prize 2023: Halik Kochanski, Resistance: The Underground War in Europe, 1939-45
items.authors: Halik Kochanski
items.summary: The UK's most valuable history prize (£50,000) went to the first English-language study of resistance to Nazi occupation across the whole of Europe, from Norway to Greece and from France to the Soviet partisan zones. Kochanski compares why resistance took such different forms (intelligence networks, sabotage, underground press, full guerrilla war) and weighs its military value against its terrible cost in reprisals, questioning the heroic national myths built after 1945. The shortlist included James Belich's The World the Plague Made and Emma Smith's Portable Magic. Later Wolfson winners were Joya Chatterji (2024) and Hannah Durkin (2025); the 2026 winner is due in December 2026.
items.headline: The Wolfson Prize recognizes a history of resistance in wartime Europe

items.title: Genomic inference of a severe human bottleneck during the Early to Middle Pleistocene transition
items.authors: Wangjie Hu, Ziqian Hao, Pengyuan Du, Fabio Di Vincenzo, Giorgio Manzi, Jialong Cui, Yun-Xin Fu, Yi-Hsuan Pan, Haipeng Li
items.summary: Using a new statistical method (FitCoal) on the genomes of 3,154 living people, the authors argued that our ancestors shrank to roughly 1,280 breeding individuals between about 930,000 and 813,000 years ago and stayed that small for around 117,000 years, nearly going extinct. The claim drew wide coverage but is disputed: independent reanalyses in Genetics (2024) and Molecular Biology and Evolution (Cousins and Durvasula, 2025) found that a model with no severe bottleneck fits the data as well or better, and that the signal may be an artifact of the method, while the original team has defended the result. It is a useful case study in how population-history inferences from modern DNA depend heavily on modelling assumptions.
items.headline: A genetic model proposes a severe bottleneck in early human ancestry

items.title: Late Yayoi stone-coffin grave and bronze-casting remains in the 'mystery area' of the Yoshinogari site, Saga
items.authors: Saga Prefecture Cultural Heritage Protection and Promotion Office
items.summary: Yoshinogari is Japan's largest Yayoi-period moated settlement, long linked in popular debate to the 'Yamatai' polity described in the Chinese Records of the Three Kingdoms. In 2023 excavators finally dug a hilltop plot that had been covered by a shrine and found the site's largest stone-coffin grave, its lids incised with cross and 'ki'-shaped marks and its floor stained with red pigment reserved for high-status burials, dated to the late 2nd-mid 3rd century CE. The coffin held no grave goods or bones, so hopes of identifying a ruler were unfulfilled, but follow-up digs in 2023-2024 uncovered bronze-casting molds and crucible fragments, some in stone types pointing to Korean Peninsula connections. Results have so far appeared in official prefectural reports rather than peer-reviewed journals.
items.headline: New finds investigate a burial and bronze working at Yoshinogari

items.title: Genetic population structure of the Xiongnu Empire at imperial and local scales
items.authors: Juhyeon Lee, Bryan K. Miller, Jamsranjav Bayarsaikhan et al.
items.summary: The Xiongnu (c. 200 BC to AD 100) were the first nomadic empire of the eastern steppe and Han China's great rival, known mostly from Chinese sources. Genome-wide data from 18 individuals in two frontier cemeteries in Mongolia show genetic diversity within single communities and even families as high as across the whole empire, with lower-status burials the most heterogeneous and the highest-status graves, often women, drawn from a narrower set of lineages. This supports the picture of a multi-ethnic empire held together by elite kin networks in which women held real political power.
items.headline: Ancient DNA reveals diversity and kinship within the Xiongnu Empire

items.title: Severe multi-year drought coincident with Hittite collapse around 1198–1196 BC
items.authors: Sturt W. Manning, Cindy Kocik, Brita Lorentzen et al.
items.summary: Ring widths and stable carbon isotopes from ancient juniper timbers in central Anatolia (from the Midas Mound tumulus at Gordion) yielded a year-by-year record of growing-season moisture. They reveal three consecutive years of extreme drought from about 1198 to 1196 BC (plus or minus 3 years), exactly when the Hittite Empire disintegrated during the wider Late Bronze Age collapse. The authors argue such back-to-back failures could overwhelm even a resilient grain-storage state, adding precise climate evidence to a debate long dominated by texts and destruction layers.
items.headline: Tree rings identify a severe drought near the Hittite collapse

items.title: Climatic and societal impacts in Scandinavia following the 536 and 540 CE volcanic double event
items.authors: Evelien van Dijk, Ingar Mørkestøl Gundersen, Anna de Bode, Helge Høeg, Kjetil Loftsgarden, Frode Iversen, Claudia Timmreck, Johann Jungclaus, Kirstin Krüger
items.summary: Two huge volcanic eruptions in 536 and 540 CE threw a sulphate veil into the stratosphere and opened the Late Antique Little Ice Age, the coldest stretch of the past two thousand years. This study ran Earth-system climate simulations for southern Norway, finding summer cooling of up to 3.5 °C, then fed the results into a growing-degree-day model to ask where barley and oats could still ripen. Mountainous western districts faced probable crop failure and show abandonment in pollen and archaeological records, while the Oslofjord lowlands stayed viable and settled, which fits the uneven pattern of farm desertion in sixth-century Scandinavia and the Norse memory of a 'Fimbulwinter'.
items.headline: Climate evidence investigates Scandinavia after sixth-century volcanic eruptions

items.title: Genome-wide data from medieval German Jews show that the Ashkenazi founder event pre-dated the 14th century
items.authors: Shamam Waldman, Daniel Backenroth, Éadaoin Harney, Stefan Flohr, ... David Reich, Shai Carmi
items.summary: Genome-wide data from 33 people buried in the 14th-century Jewish cemetery of Erfurt, Germany (sampled from loose teeth with the consent of the local Jewish community) show they were already genetically very close to modern Ashkenazi Jews. The 'founder event' - a sharp population bottleneck that explains why certain hereditary diseases are common among Ashkenazim today - therefore happened before 1350, and a third of the Erfurt individuals already carried a mitochondrial lineage common in Ashkenazi Jews today. The Erfurt group was also more varied in Eastern European-related ancestry than its modern descendants, hinting at two sub-communities that later merged.
items.headline: Medieval Jewish genomes help date an Ashkenazi population bottleneck

items.title: New discoveries at the Sanxingdui Bronze Age site in south-west China
items.authors: Yingfu Li, Tian Qiu, Jianbo Guo, Yuniu Li
items.summary: Six new sacrificial pits (Pits 3-8) were found beside the two famous pits excavated in 1986 at Sanxingdui in Sichuan, the center of the Bronze Age Shu culture. Radiocarbon dates place most pits around 1200-1000 BCE, contemporary with the late Shang capital at Anyang, with Pits 5 and 6 slightly later. Finds include a 280-gram gold mask, bronze figures and altars unlike anything from the Shang heartland, bamboo textiles and hundreds of elephant tusks; by 2024 over 13,000 catalogued objects had come out of the new pits. The discoveries reinforce the view that early Chinese civilization was a network of distinct regional cultures rather than a single Central Plains core, although why the objects were smashed, burned and buried remains debated.
items.headline: Sanxingdui excavations reveal more of a distinctive Bronze Age culture

items.title: Evolution of immune genes is associated with the Black Death
items.authors: Jennifer Klunk, Tauras P. Vilgalys, Christian E. Demeure, ... Luis B. Barreiro, Hendrik N. Poinar
items.summary: Ancient DNA from 206 people buried in London and Denmark before, during and after the 1348-49 plague suggested that variants in immune genes, especially ERAP2, rose sharply in frequency among survivors, implying the Black Death acted as a powerful episode of natural selection with echoes in modern autoimmune disease risk. In February 2025 Barton, Santander, Skoglund, Moltke, Reich and Mathieson published a Matters Arising in Nature (doi 10.1038/s41586-024-08496-5) arguing that the enrichment vanishes under a proper randomization test, that an allele-frequency error removed all four candidate loci once corrected, and that ERAP2 shows no selection signal across 2,000 years of European genomes. The original team replied and stands by ERAP2 on functional grounds, so the claim is live but contested.
items.headline: A study links immune-gene changes with the Black Death

items.title: Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2022 awarded to Svante Pääbo for the genomes of extinct hominins
items.authors: Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institutet (laureate: Svante Pääbo, Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology)
items.summary: Pääbo was honoured 'for his discoveries concerning the genomes of extinct hominins and human evolution': the first Neanderthal genome (2010), the discovery of the Denisovans from a finger bone, and proof that both interbred with modern humans, so that most people today carry a small share of Neanderthal DNA. The Nobel citation credits him with founding paleogenomics, the recovery and analysis of ancient DNA, which is now a standard tool for reconstructing migrations, kinship and disease in the past. The award marked mainstream recognition that genetics had become a primary historical source.
items.headline: The medicine Nobel honors Pääbo's work on extinct human genomes

items.title: Genomes from a medieval mass burial show Ashkenazi-associated hereditary diseases pre-date the 12th century
items.authors: Selina Brace, Yoan Diekmann, Thomas Booth, Ruairidh Macleod, ... Mark G. Thomas, Ian Barnes
items.summary: At least seventeen people, many of them children, were found in 2004 at the bottom of a medieval well in Norwich, England, during the Chapelfield shopping-centre excavation. Genomes from six of them show closest affinity to modern Ashkenazi Jews, and revised radiocarbon dates fit the recorded antisemitic massacre of Norwich's Jews on 6 February 1190, at the start of the Third Crusade. The individuals already carried disease variants now concentrated in Ashkenazi populations, pushing the origin of those traits back before 1200 and turning an archaeological puzzle into evidence for a documented medieval atrocity.
items.headline: A medieval mass burial provides evidence about Ashkenazi ancestry and disease variants

items.title: The genetic history of the Southern Arc: A bridge between West Asia and Europe
items.authors: Iosif Lazaridis, Songül Alpaslan-Roodenberg, Ayşe Acar et al.
items.summary: Analysis of 727 ancient genomes from Anatolia, the Caucasus, the Balkans and the Levant spanning 10,000 years tracked Chalcolithic and Bronze Age migrations, including the spread of Yamnaya steppe pastoralists into the Balkans and Caucasus. Ancient DNA (genetic material recovered from old bones and teeth) showed Bronze Age Anatolians had little or no steppe ancestry, so the authors proposed that the Anatolian branch of Indo-European arrived by a different route and that the 'Indo-Anatolian' homeland lay in West Asia. The linguistic conclusions remain debated among linguists and geneticists.
items.headline: Southern Arc genomes illuminate connections between West Asia and Europe

items.title: Northeastern Asian and Jomon-related genetic structure in the Three Kingdoms period of Gimhae, Korea
items.authors: Pere Gelabert, Asta Blazyte, Yongjoon Chang, Daniel M. Fernandes, Sungwon Jeon et al.
items.summary: Eight genomes from 4th-5th century CE burials at Gimhae, capital of the Gaya confederacy in southeastern Korea during the Three Kingdoms period, are the first ancient genomes from Korea's Three Kingdoms period. The individuals descended from a mix of northern Chinese Bronze Age ancestry and a Jomon-related component otherwise associated with prehistoric Japan, and they fell into two genetic groups within one elite cemetery. Modern Koreans are nearly continuous with these people over 1,700 years but have since lost most of the Jomon-like ancestry. The findings show that Japan and Korea shared population history in both directions, not just Korea-to-Japan migration.
items.headline: Ancient genomes investigate ancestry in Three Kingdoms Korea

items.title: Palaeoecological data indicates land-use changes across Europe linked to spatial heterogeneity in mortality during the Black Death pandemic
items.authors: Adam Izdebski, Piotr Guzowski, Radosław Poniat, Lucrezia Masci, Jessie Palmer, ... Timothy P. Newfield et al.
items.summary: Using fossil pollen from 261 radiocarbon-dated lake and wetland cores in 19 countries, the team tracked whether farmland reverted to wild vegetation after 1347-52, a proxy for how many farmers died. Cereal pollen collapsed in some regions (parts of Scandinavia, France, Germany, Greece, central Italy) but stayed flat or even rose in others (Ireland, Iberia, central-eastern Europe), so the authors argue the Black Death did not kill a uniform half of Europe. A 2022 Matters Arising countered that falling grain pollen shows population decline but not necessarily plague mortality, and the authors replied; the regional-variation result is widely cited but its scale remains debated.
items.headline: Pollen records suggest the Black Death's demographic effects varied across Europe

items.title: Collapse of the Liangzhu and other Neolithic cultures in the lower Yangtze region in response to climate change
items.authors: Haiwei Zhang, Hai Cheng, Ashish Sinha, Christoph Spötl, Yanjun Cai et al.
items.summary: Liangzhu, a UNESCO-listed Neolithic city near Hangzhou with the world's oldest known large-scale hydraulic system (dams, levees and canals, c. 3300-2300 BCE), disappeared abruptly around 4,300 years ago. Precisely dated cave stalagmite records (speleothems) show a short, anomalously wet interval at exactly that time, which the authors argue overwhelmed the water-control works and flooded the city, followed by a prolonged drought from about 4,000 years ago that undermined successor cultures. They tie both swings to intensified El Niño activity. The climate trigger is widely accepted for Liangzhu, though some archaeologists stress internal social and economic strains alongside flooding.
items.headline: Climate evidence links flooding with the decline of Liangzhu settlements

items.title: Evidence for European presence in the Americas in AD 1021
items.authors: Margot Kuitems, Birgitta L. Wallace, Charles Lindsay, Andrea Scifo, Petra Doeve, ... Michael W. Dee
items.summary: Three pieces of wood from the Norse site at L'Anse aux Meadows, Newfoundland, each cut with metal tools the Indigenous population did not use, were dated to exactly 1021 CE. The trick was a cosmic-ray spike in atmospheric radiocarbon in 993 CE that leaves a marker ring in every tree alive at the time; counting outward from that ring to the bark edge gives a calendar year rather than a broad range. This is the first precise date for Europeans in the Americas, roughly matching the Vinland sagas, though it dates one felling season and not the settlement's full span.
items.headline: Dated wood establishes a Norse presence in North America in 1021

items.title: Retraction Note: Complex societies precede moralizing gods throughout world history
items.authors: Harvey Whitehouse, Pieter François, Patrick E. Savage, Thomas E. Currie, Kevin C. Feeney, et al., Peter Turchin
items.summary: In 2019 a Nature paper using the Seshat Global History Databank, a large coded dataset of past societies, claimed that belief in punishing 'big gods' appeared only after societies grew complex, reversing a popular theory that such beliefs helped build large societies. A 2021 critique by Beheim and colleagues showed that missing data had been treated as evidence that moralizing gods were absent, and that the result flipped when the gaps were handled differently; the authors retracted the paper in July 2021 while maintaining that reanalysis still supported their conclusion, which they republished in Religion, Brain & Behavior in 2022. The episode is the clearest test to date of 'big data' comparative history and shows both its promise and how much rests on coding decisions.
items.headline: A paper connecting complex societies and moralizing gods is retracted

items.title: China, Europe, and the Great Divergence: A Restatement
items.authors: Stephen Broadberry, Hanhui Guan, David Daokui Li
items.summary: The 'Great Divergence' is the debate over when and why Europe's living standards pulled ahead of China's. Broadberry, Guan and Li's 2018 national-accounting estimates of Chinese GDP per capita from 980 to 1850 argued that China led the world under the Northern Song but fell behind Italy by 1300 and that the leading region of China (the Yangzi Delta) matched the leading regions of Europe until about 1700, after which it declined under the Qing. This 2021 restatement answers critics, notably Kent Deng and Patrick O'Brien, by revising Ming-era GDP down by roughly a tenth to a seventh while keeping the c. 1700 divergence date. The dating still splits the field: the 'California School' (Pomeranz) puts divergence after 1800, while Deng and O'Brien question whether Chinese sources can support any GDP series at all.
items.headline: A historian revisits why Europe and China followed different economic paths

items.title: The IntCal20 Northern Hemisphere Radiocarbon Age Calibration Curve (0–55 cal kBP)
items.authors: Paula J. Reimer, William E. N. Austin, Edouard Bard, Alex Bayliss, Paul G. Blackwell, et al. (IntCal Working Group)
items.summary: Radiocarbon dates are not calendar dates: the amount of carbon-14 in the atmosphere has wobbled over time, so every raw radiocarbon age must be converted using a calibration curve built from tree rings, cave deposits, corals and lake sediments of known age. IntCal20 is the current international standard, replacing IntCal13 and extending back 55,000 years with new statistical methods and thousands of new measurements. Because nearly every archaeological date since 2020 is calibrated against it, this one paper quietly shifted published chronologies for the Neolithic, the Bronze Age (including the Thera eruption debate) and early human dispersals by decades to centuries.
items.headline: An updated calibration curve improves the interpretation of radiocarbon dates

items.title: The Justinianic Plague: An inconsequential pandemic?
items.authors: Lee Mordechai, Merle Eisenberg, Timothy P. Newfield et al.
items.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
items.summary: The Justinianic Plague (AD 541-750) is traditionally credited with killing tens of millions and ending the ancient world. Mordechai and colleagues checked that claim against written sources, laws, coins, papyri, inscriptions, pollen, ancient DNA and burials, and found none independently showed mass mortality, concluding the plague was not a major driver of late antique change. The paper triggered a sustained debate: Mischa Meier (2020) and Peter Sarris (Past & Present, 2021) argued the authors underweighted legal, numismatic and genetic evidence, and the significance of the pandemic remains genuinely contested.
items.headline: A reassessment questions claims about the Justinianic Plague's scale
